translations.text: Holy teachers have counselled that the faithful Church should celebrate this day in honour of All Saints, and keep it as a festival with reverence;
because they could not appoint a separate feast day for each of them, nor are the names of them all known to anyone in this present life, as John the Evangelist wrote in his spiritual vision,
saying thus: "I saw so great a multitude that no one can number it, from all nations and from every tribe, standing before God's throne,
all clothed in white garments, holding palm branches in their hands, and they sang with a loud voice: 'Salvation be to our God, who sits upon his throne.'
"And all the angels stood around his throne, and bowed down to God, saying thus: Blessing and brightness, wisdom and thanksgiving, honour and strength be to our God, for ever and ever. Amen."
God's saints are angels and men. Angels are spirits without bodies. The Almighty Ruler created them in great beauty, for his own praise, and for the glory and honour of his majesty for ever.
We are afraid to say much about them, because it is for God alone to know how their invisible nature continues in eternal purity, without any defilement or diminishing.
Nevertheless we learn from the holy scriptures that there are nine hosts of angels dwelling in heavenly majesty, who have never committed any sin.
The tenth host was lost through pride, and they were turned into accursed spirits, and thrust out of heavenly joy into hellish torment.
Truly some of the holy spirits who remained with their Creator come to us as messengers, and make known things to come. Some of them, by God's ordinance, work signs and frequent miracles on earth.
Some of them are set as rulers over the other angels, to fulfil the divine mysteries. Through some, God establishes and determines his judgments.
Some of them are so closely joined to God that there are no others between them and him, and they burn with love all the greater, the more keenly they behold God's brightness.
Now this day is reverently hallowed to these angels, and also to the holy men who, through great merits, have prospered with God since the beginning of the world.
Of these the first were the patriarchs, devout and glorious men in their lives, the fathers of the prophets, whose memory will not be forgotten, and whose name endures for ever;
because they were pleasing to God through faith, and righteousness, and obedience. After these follows the chosen company of the prophets:
They were God's spokesmen, and to them he revealed his secrets. He enlightened them with the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that they knew the things to come and proclaimed them in prophetic song.
Truly, the chosen prophets shone in their lives through many signs and prefigurations. They healed people's sicknesses and raised the bodies of the dead to life.

They also withheld the showers of heaven because of the people's perversity, and afterwards, having mercy, granted them again. They lamented the people's sins, and warded off the punishment of those sins upon themselves.
Taught by the Holy Spirit, they prophesied Christ's incarnation, his passion, his resurrection, his ascension, and the great judgment.
In the New Testament came John the Baptist, who proclaimed Christ's coming by prophecy and also pointed him out with his finger.
"Among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist."
With these champions of God agrees the twelvefold number of Christ's apostles, whom he himself chose as his disciples and trained in right faith and true teaching,
and appointed as teachers to all nations, so that the sound of their preaching went throughout all the earth, and their words reached to the ends of the whole world.
To these twelve apostles the Almighty Saviour said, "You are the light of the world:
let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven. You are my friends, and I make known to you whatever I have heard from my Father."
Truly the Lord gave power to his twelve apostles, so that they worked the same miracles that he himself performed on earth.
And whatever they bind on earth is bound in heaven; and whatever they loose on earth is loosed in heaven.
He also gave them a true promise that at the great Judgment they will sit on twelve judgment-seats, to judge all people who have ever received life in the body.
After the company of the apostles we honour the steadfast host of God's martyrs, who bravely imitated Christ's passion through various torments and went to the heavenly kingdom through martyrdom.
Some were killed with weapons, some burned up in flames, others beaten with whips, others pierced with stakes,
some were killed on the gallows, some were sunk in the wide sea, others were flayed alive, others were torn apart with iron claws, some were crushed with stones,
some tormented by winter cold, some killed by hunger, and some had their hands and feet cut off as a spectacle for the people, for the faith and for the holy name of Christ the Saviour.
These are the victorious friends of God, who scorned the commands of the guilty rulers, and now they are crowned with glory, with the victory of their sufferings, in eternal joy.
Their bodies could be killed, but no tortures could turn them away from God. Their hope was full of immortality, even though they were tortured in front of men.

They were afflicted for a short time and comforted for a long time, because God tested them like gold in a furnace, and he found them worthy of himself, and he received them into his heavenly kingdom like holy offerings.

After the persecution by cruel kings and rulers had ended, when God's church lived in peace, there were holy priests who flourished for God, and who always turned the people to God with true teaching and holy examples.
Their minds were pure and filled with chastity, and with clean hands they served God Almighty at his altar, celebrating the holy mysteries of Christ's body and his blood.
They also offered themselves to God as a living sacrifice, without blemish or any mixture of perverse work.

They entrusted God's teaching to those placed under them, as a loan that would earn unfailing interest, and with rebuke and prayer and great care they turned their minds to the way of life, and no worldly fear made them keep silent about God's law;

and even though they did not feel the edge of the sword, the merits of their lives mean they are not deprived of martyrdom, because martyrdom is achieved not only by shedding blood, but also by abstaining from sins and by keeping God's commandments.
After these follows the way of life of the anchorites, with their singular devotion. Living in deserts, they trampled down worldly pleasures and lusts with strong minds and strict lives.
They fled from the sight and praise of worldly people. Hiding in poor caves or huts, they lived alongside wild beasts and grew used to speaking with angels, and they shone with great miracles.
They gave sight to the blind, the power to walk to the lame, hearing to the deaf, and speech to the mute. They overcame devils and drove them out, and through God's power they raised the dead.
The book called Vitae Patrum (Lives of the Fathers) speaks at length about the way of life of these anchorites, and also of monks living in community, and says,
that there were many thousands of them everywhere, in deserts and in monasteries, living wonderful lives, but mostly in Egypt.
Some lived on fruit and herbs, some by their own labour; angels served some of them, and birds served others, until at last, at a gentle death, angels carried them to God.
O blessed Mother of God, Mary ever virgin, temple of the Holy Spirit, virgin before conceiving, virgin in conceiving, virgin after conceiving,
great is your glory on this feast day among the saints already mentioned, because through your pure childbearing holiness and heavenly honours came to them all.

We speak of the heavenly Queen in her proper order, as fits her womanhood; yet the whole faithful church faithfully sings of her that she is exalted and raised above the hosts of angels to the glorious throne.
It is not said of any other saint that any of them is raised above the hosts of angels, except of Mary alone.
Through her example she showed the heavenly life on earth, because virginity is the queen of all virtues and the companion of the heavenly angels.

Following the examples and footsteps of this virgin, a countless company of virgins persevered in chastity, gave up marriage, and joined themselves with steadfast minds to the heavenly bridegroom, Christ,

and holy conduct, and modest clothing, so much so that a great many of them suffered martyrdom for the sake of their virginity, and so, with a twofold victory, they came in glory to the heavenly dwellings.

To all these saints mentioned before, that is, to the angels and to God's chosen people, the honour of this day is celebrated in the faithful Church, to their honour and to our help, so that through their intercession we may be joined in fellowship with them.
May the merciful Lord grant us this, who redeemed them all, and us, with his precious blood from the captivity of the devil.
On this glorious feast we ought to make up, with holy prayers and hymns of praise, for whatever we observed
less fully on the other feast-days of the whole course of the year because of human frailty, and we ought to take careful thought that we may come to the eternal feast.
Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up onto a mountain, and so on.
The holy gospel that was read before you a little while ago agrees closely with this feast, because it sets out in order the eight beatitudes that brought the saints to heavenly honours.
Matthew wrote in today's gospel that the Saviour at one time "saw a great multitude following him; then he went up onto a mountain.
When he had sat down, his disciples came to him, and he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: "Blessed are the poor in spirit," and so on.

The wise Augustine expounded this gospel and said that the mountain the Saviour went up signifies the lofty commandments of true righteousness; the lesser commandments were laid down for the Jewish people.
Yet it was the one God who, through his holy prophets, set the lesser commandments for the Jewish people, who were still bound by fear;

and through his own Son he set the greater commandments for the Christian people, whom he came to redeem out of true love. He taught while sitting, which belongs to the dignity of the teacher's office.
His disciples came to him," so that those who drew near to his commandments in mind were nearer to him in body. "The Saviour opened his mouth."
Truly he opened his mouth for the teaching of the gospel, he who in the old law customarily opened the mouths of the prophets.
Yet the opening of his mouth signifies the profound speech that he then brought forth. He said, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
Who are the poor in spirit but the humble, who have the fear of God and have no pride?
The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, and pride is the beginning of every sin. Many are poor through lack of possessions and not in their spirit, because they desire to have much.
There are also others who are poor, not through lack of possessions but in spirit, because they are, according to the apostle's saying, "as having nothing, and possessing all things."
In this way Abraham was poor, and Jacob, and David, who, though raised up on his royal throne, showed himself to be poor in spirit, saying thus: "Truly I am needy and poor."
The proud rich are not poor, neither through want nor in spirit, because they are enriched with possessions and puffed up in mind.

Poor both through lack of possessions and in spirit are the perfect monks, who for God's sake give up all things so completely that they will not have even their own bodies in their own control, but live by the direction of their spiritual teachers;
and therefore, as greatly as they live here in poverty for God's sake, so greatly will they afterwards be enriched in the glory to come.
"Blessed are the gentle, for they shall possess the land." Those are gentle and meek who do not resist the evil, but overcome the evil one with their goodness:
they shall have the land of which the psalmist spoke: "Lord, you are my hope; be my portion in the land of the living."
The land of the living is the stability of the eternal homeland, in which the soul rests as the body rests in the earth. That homeland is the rest and life of the chosen saints.
"Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." Those who mourn over the injuries or losses of transitory goods are not blessed;
but those are blessed who bewail their sins, because the Holy Spirit, who grants forgiveness of all sins, comforts them,
He is called Paraclete, that is, Comforter, because he comforts the hearts of the penitent through his grace.
"Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled."
He hungers and thirsts after righteousness who gladly hears God's commandments, and more gladly fulfils them in deeds.
he will then be filled with the food of which the Lord spoke: "My food is that I do my Father's will"; that is, righteousness.
Then he may say with the psalmist: "Lord, I shall appear with righteousness in your sight, and I shall be filled when your glory is revealed."
"Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy."
Blessed are those who help poor people out of mercy, for they will be rewarded in such a way that they themselves will be set free from misery.
"Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God himself."
Foolish are those who desire to see God with fleshly eyes, when he is seen with the heart; but the heart must be cleansed of sins so that it may see God.
Just as earthly light cannot be seen except with clean eyes, so too God is not seen except with a clean heart.
"Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God."
Perfection lies in peace, where nothing is at odds; therefore the peaceable are God's children, because nothing in them strives against God.
Those are peaceable within themselves who order all the stirrings of their mind by reason and subdue their fleshly desires, so that they themselves become God's kingdom.
This is the peace that is given on earth to people of good will. God our Father is peaceable; truly, therefore, it is fitting for the children to imitate their Father.
"Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
There are many who suffer persecution for various causes, as murderers do, and robbers, and every kind of wicked person;
but that persecution does not bring them to any blessedness; only the persecution that is suffered for righteousness' sake brings one to eternal blessedness.
The persecution of perverse people is not to be feared, but rather to be patiently endured, as the Lord said to his disciples: "Do not fear those who kill your body,
for they cannot kill your soul; but fear God, who can destroy both soul and body in the torment of hell."
Yet we should not provoke the perverse into persecuting us, but rather, if they are stirred up, calm them with righteousness.
If, however, they will not stop the persecution, it is better for us to suffer persecution than to forsake what is right.
Eight beatitudes are set out in order in this gospel; yet there is still one saying after them, which seems as if it were the ninth step,
but in truth it belongs to the eighth beatitude, because both of them speak of persecution for righteousness' sake and for Christ's.
The eight beatitudes apply to all faithful people, and the last saying, though it was spoken specifically to the apostles, [?]
it also applies to all the members of Christ, because it is not the ninth, but follows on from the eighth beatitude, as we said before.
The Saviour said, "Blessed are you when people curse you and persecute you and falsely speak every evil against you for my sake."
He is blessed and happy who for Christ's sake suffers cursing and insults from false hypocrites, for the false cursing turns into a blessed benediction for the righteous.
"Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven."
It is fitting for the faithful to glory in tribulations, because tribulation produces patience, and patience produces proof, and proof produces hope.
Truly, hope is never put to shame, because the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is given to us.
Of this the apostle James said, "O my brothers, count it all joy when you are in various temptations, because the testing of your faith is much more precious than gold that is tested by fire."
Again the holy scripture says, "Earthen vessels are tested in the furnace, and righteous men in the tribulation of their temptation."
Of this the Saviour also said in another place to his disciples, "If this world hates you, know that it hated me before you;
and if they persecuted me, then they will also persecute you." Christ himself was killed by wicked men, and so also were his disciples and martyrs;
and all those who desire to live piously in the faithful Church must suffer persecution, either from the invisible devil or from the visible wicked limbs of the devil.
But we must endure these temporary persecutions or tribulations with joy for Christ's name, because he promised thus to all the patient: "Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is manifold in heaven."
We could expound this holy reading more fully, following Augustine's interpretation, but we doubt whether you can usefully understand any greater depth in it;
but let us pray with inward heart to the Almighty Ruler, who has gladdened us today with the manifold celebration of all his saints,
that he may grant us an abundance of his mercy through their manifold intercessions, so that we may rejoice with him in the eternal vision, just as we now honour them with temporal service.
Glory and praise be to the Saviour Christ, who is the beginning and the end, Creator and Redeemer of all saints, with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, ever into eternity. Amen.
